extracted.intended_audience: employers, human resources professionals, labor compliance officers, and employment/labor counsel interpreting FLSA white-collar exemptions
extracted.subtask_description: Determine whether employees qualify as exempt under 29 CFR part 541 (executive, administrative, professional, outside sales, and highly compensated exemptions), including salary/compensation tests, salary-basis rules, duties/primary-duty tests, and related definitions and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drivers who may qualify as exempt outside sales employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Drivers who provide the only sales contact between the employer and the customers visited; who call on customers and take orders for products; who deliver products from stock in the employee's vehicle or procure and deliver the product later; and who receive compensation commensurate with the volume of products sold; drivers who obtain or solicit orders from persons with authority to commit purchases; drivers who call on new prospects along route and attempt to secure regular delivery agreements; drivers who call on established customers and persuade them to accept increased amounts or new products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists four illustrative categories (¶ (1)–(4)) of drivers that may qualify as outside sales employees, describing sales contact, order solicitation, delivery tied to sales, calling on prospects, and persuading established customers. Use these functional facts to evaluate whether a driver is performing outside sales exempt work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drivers who generally would not qualify as exempt outside sales employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Route drivers whose primary duty is stocking and servicing vending machines; drivers who repeatedly call on established customers delivering products where sale amount is not significantly affected by driver solicitation or is determined by customer volume since prior delivery; drivers primarily engaged in deliveries and promotional activities (placing advertising, price stamping, arranging merchandise, rotating stock, cleaning/service of display cases) unless such work furthers the driver's own sales efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides three illustrative scenarios (¶ (1)–(3)) of nonqualifying drivers; use these to distinguish delivery/merchandising-focused roles from true outside sales duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard salary level for executive/administrative/professional exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as an exempt executive, administrative, or professional employee under section 13(a)(1) of the Act, an employee must be compensated on a salary basis at a rate per week of not less than the amounts set forth in ¶ (a)(1)–(3), exclusive of board, lodging or other facilities, unless exceptions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies amounts and effective dates: $844/week beginning July 1, 2024 (20th percentile benchmark); $1,128/week beginning Jan 1, 2025 (35th percentile); and a level as of July 1, 2027 calculated pursuant to §541.607(b)(1). Notes administrative/professional employees may alternatively be paid on a fee basis (§541.605).

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial salary level exceptions (CNMI, Guam, Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Guam, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands (employed by non-Federal employers) must be compensated on a salary basis at a rate of not less than $455 per week to qualify as exempt executive/administrative/professional employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States $455/week applies in those territories and that administrative and professional employees may also be paid on a fee basis (§541.605).

rubrics_metrics.name: American Samoa salary level exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees in American Samoa (employed by non-Federal employers) must be compensated on a salary basis at a rate of not less than $380 per week to qualify as exempt executive/administrative/professional employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes administrative and professional employees in American Samoa may also be paid on a fee basis (§541.605).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of payment equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The weekly salary level requirement may be translated into equivalent amounts for pay periods longer than one week; the shortest period of payment that meets the requirement is one week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives conversion examples for the $1,128/week requirement (biweekly $2,256; semimonthly $2,444; monthly $4,888) and cautions that one week is the shortest qualifying payment period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative salary level for academic administrative employees
rubrics_metrics.description: For academic administrative employees, the salary level requirement may be met by compensation at a rate at least equal to the entrance salary for teachers in the educational establishment employing the administrative employee, per §541.204(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an alternative way academic administrators can meet the salary test based on institution's teacher entrance salary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hourly rate option for certain computer employees
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of computer employees, the compensation requirement may be met by hourly pay at a rate not less than $27.63 an hour (per §541.400(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies that computer employees have an allowed hourly compensation threshold alternative to salary/fee basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to the standard salary criteria for certain professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: The compensation requirements in this section do not apply to employees engaged as teachers; employees who hold a valid license or certificate permitting the practice of law or medicine and are actually engaged in practice thereof; or employees who hold the requisite academic degree for general practice of medicine and are in internship or residency programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains professional exceptions and notes that the exception does not extend to many medical occupations (pharmacists, nurses, therapists, technologists, sanitarians, dietitians, social workers, psychologists, psychometrists, or other professions servicing the medical profession).

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly compensated employee (HCE) test and thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee is exempt as a highly compensated employee under section 13(a)(1) if the employee receives total annual compensation at least equal to the amounts in ¶ (a)(1)–(4) and customarily and regularly performs any one or more of the exempt duties or responsibilities of an executive, administrative, or professional employee identified in subparts B, C, or D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States thresholds: $132,964/year beginning July 1, 2024 (80th percentile); $151,164/year beginning Jan 1, 2025 (85th percentile); a level as of July 1, 2027 per §541.607(b)(2). Also ¶ (a)(4) covers proportional determination when multiple compensation levels apply during a year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components and calculation of total annual compensation for HCE
rubrics_metrics.description: Total annual compensation must include at least a weekly amount equal to the amount required by §541.600(a)(1)–(3) paid on a salary or fee basis, and may include commissions, nondiscretionary bonuses and other nondiscretionary compensation earned during a 52-week period; it does not include board, lodging, other facilities, medical/life insurance payments, retirement contributions, or other fringe benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes rule that §541.602(a)(3) does not apply to HCEs and clarifies excluded compensation categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final payment rule to achieve HCE threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employee's total annual compensation falls short of the HCE minimum by the last pay period of the 52-week period, the employer may make one final payment during the last pay period or within one month after the end of the 52-week period to achieve the required level; such payment counts only toward the prior year's total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an illustrative example where employer makes a post-year payment to reach required HCE level; notes failure to make such payment means employee does not qualify as HCE but may still qualify under other exemption tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro rata rule for employees not working a full year
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee who does not work a full year may qualify for the HCE exemption if the employee receives a pro rata portion of the minimum amount based on number of weeks employed; employer may make one final payment within one month after end of employment as under the general final payment rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows proportional application of HCE threshold for partial-year employees and use of final payment remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of 52-week period for HCE calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer may utilize any 52-week period as the 'year' (calendar, fiscal, or anniversary of hire); if not identified in advance, the calendar year applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives employer flexibility in selecting the 52-week period used to compute total annual compensation for HCE purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: High compensation as strong indicator reducing duties analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A high level of compensation is a strong indicator of exempt status, eliminating need for detailed duties analysis; a HCE will qualify if the employee customarily and regularly performs any one or more exempt duties or responsibilities identified in subparts B, C, or D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a HCE who customarily directs work of two or more employees may qualify as an exempt executive even if other executive requirements are not all met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: HCE section applies only to office or non-manual work
rubrics_metrics.description: Section applies only to employees whose primary duty includes performing office or non-manual work; non-management production-line and non-management employees engaged in manual, repetitive operations are not exempt under this section regardless of pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists occupations commonly excluded (carpenters, electricians, mechanics, plumbers, iron workers, craftsmen, operating engineers, longshoremen, construction workers, laborers) as examples of nonexempt manual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary basis general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee is paid on a 'salary basis' if they regularly receive each pay period a predetermined amount constituting all or part of compensation, which is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of work performed; subject to specified exceptions, an exempt employee must receive full salary for any week in which the employee performs any work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes that exempt employees need not be paid for weeks they perform no work; and an employee is not paid on a salary basis if deductions are made for absences occasioned by the employer or operating requirements when employee is ready, willing, and able to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial satisfaction of salary by nondiscretionary bonuses/incentives (10% rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Up to ten percent of the salary amount required by §541.600(a)–(c) may be satisfied by payment of nondiscretionary bonuses, incentives, and commissions that are paid annually or more frequently; employer may use any 52-week period as the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies that if by the last pay period of the 52-week period sum of weekly salary plus nondiscretionary payments is less than 52 times the weekly salary amount, the employer may make one final payment within the next pay period to meet the requirement; provision does not apply to HCEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions permitting deductions from salary
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition against deductions from pay in the salary basis requirement is subject to exceptions including: (1) full-day absences for personal reasons (other than sickness/disability); (2) full-day absences for sickness/disability if made in accordance with a bona fide plan/policy; (3) offsetting jury/witness/military pay against salary for that week; (4) penalties for infractions of safety rules of major significance; (5) unpaid disciplinary suspensions of one or more full days imposed in good faith under a written policy applicable to all employees; (6) proportionate pay for initial/terminal weeks; (7) proportionate pay for weeks with unpaid FMLA leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples for how exceptions operate (e.g., partial-day personal absences only allow deduction for full days; example of short-term disability plan timing; jury/witness offsets; examples of safety-rule and disciplinary suspension applications; pay treatment in initial/terminal or FMLA weeks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of allowed deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: When calculating an allowed deduction under the exceptions, the employer may use the hourly or daily equivalent of the employee's full weekly salary or any other amount proportional to the time actually missed; deduction for safety-rule penalties may be any amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies practical methods for computing permitted deductions under ¶ (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of improper deductions from salary
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer who makes improper deductions from salary shall lose the exemption if facts demonstrate the employer did not intend to pay employees on a salary basis; an actual practice of making improper deductions demonstrates lack of intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists factors to consider (number of improper deductions, time period, number and geographic location of employees affected, number/locations of managers responsible, whether employer has clearly communicated policy). Explains that loss of exemption applies during the time improper deductions were made for employees in the same job classification working for same managers; isolated or inadvertent improper deductions will not result in loss if employer reimburses employees. A clearly communicated written policy with complaint mechanism, reimbursement, and good faith commitment to comply will prevent loss unless the employer willfully continues improper deductions after complaints; best evidence is a written policy distributed prior to deductions. Also states this section is not to be construed in unduly technical manner to defeat the exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum guarantee plus extras rule
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer may provide an exempt employee with additional compensation without losing the exemption if the employment arrangement includes a guarantee of at least the minimum weekly-required amount paid on a salary basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: under the $1,128/week requirement, a guaranteed $1,128/week plus a 1% commission is permissible. An exempt employee guaranteed the weekly salary may also receive percentages of sales or profits, or compensation for work beyond the normal workweek on any basis (flat sum, bonus, straight-time hourly, overtime, etc.), including paid time off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hourly/daily/shift computed earnings with reasonable relationship test
rubrics_metrics.description: An exempt employee's earnings may be computed on an hourly, daily or shift basis without losing the exemption if the arrangement includes a guarantee of at least the minimum weekly required amount paid on a salary basis and a reasonable relationship exists between the guaranteed amount and the amount actually earned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable relationship met if weekly guarantee roughly equivalent to usual earnings at assigned rate for normal scheduled workweek. Provides an example: guarantee of $1,210/week with normal 4–5 shifts per week and $350/shift pay meets $1,128/week requirement. Test applies only when pay is computed hourly/daily/shift and not to guarantees combined with commissions/profits that may exceed guarantee in some weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee basis payment for administrative/professional employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative and professional employees may be paid on a fee basis (agreed sum for a single job regardless of time required). Fees resemble piecework but are for a unique job rather than repeated series of identical jobs; payments based on hours/days are not fee basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine whether a fee meets the minimum salary requirement, test the fee by the time worked on the job and whether the fee amounts to at least the minimum salary per week if the employee worked 40 hours (example: $600 for a picture taking 20 hours equals $1,200 for 40 hours and meets $1,128/week requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board, lodging, or other facilities excluded from minimum salary calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for exemption, the employee must earn the minimum salary 'exclusive of board, lodging or other facilities' — costs to employer for non-cash items of value may not count toward the minimum salary amount required for exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains 'exclusive of board, lodging or other facilities' means 'free and clear' of any claimed credit for non-cash items. References 29 CFR part 531 for definitions and gives examples (meals furnished by company cafeterias, dormitory rooms, tuition furnished by colleges, merchandise at company stores, housing for dwelling purposes, ordinary commuting transportation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular updates to salary and compensation amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial update set amounts (standard salary $844/week and HCE $132,964/year beginning July 1, 2024) and prescribes that as of July 1, 2027 and every 3 years thereafter, amounts will be updated to reflect current earnings data using the methodology in effect when Secretary issues notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary will publish notice in Federal Register not fewer than 150 days before each future update, based on most recent 4 quarters of CPS MORG data (or successor). Wage and Hour Division will publish updated amounts on its website by effective date. There is a 120-day delay mechanism if a separate NPRM proposing changes has been published not fewer than 150 days before update date; if no final rule is issued by end of extension, updated amounts take effect upon expiration of 120-day period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary duty test
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for exemption, an employee's 'primary duty' must be the performance of exempt work; 'primary duty' means the principal, main, major or most important duty performed and must be determined based on all facts with emphasis on the character of the job as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include relative importance of exempt duties compared with other types of duties; amount of time spent performing exempt work; employee's relative freedom from direct supervision; and relationship between employee's salary and wages paid to other employees for nonexempt work. Time spent (e.g., more than 50% performing exempt work) is a useful guide but not dispositive; examples (assistant managers) illustrate how management duties may be primary even if more than 50% time is nonexempt, while close supervision and low pay compared to nonexempt employees weigh against primary-duty conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'customarily and regularly'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase means a frequency greater than occasional but may be less than constant; includes work normally and recurrently performed every workweek and does not include isolated or one-time tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this frequency standard when assessing duties performed with regularity as part of exemption tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'exempt work'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'exempt work' means all work described in §§541.100, 541.101, 541.200, 541.300, 541.301, 541.302, 541.303, 541.304, 541.400 and 541.500, and activities directly and closely related to such work; all other work is considered 'nonexempt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to the substantive sections describing executive, administrative, professional, computer, and outside sales duties and to the 'directly and closely related' concept for borderline activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'directly and closely related' work
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that is 'directly and closely related' to the performance of exempt work is also considered exempt; the phrase means tasks related to exempt duties that contribute to or facilitate performance of exempt work and may include physical/menial tasks arising out of exempt duties and routine work without which exempt work cannot be properly performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples of such tasks (recordkeeping; monitoring and adjusting machinery; taking notes; using a computer to create documents or presentations; opening mail for reading and decisionmaking; using a photocopier or fax machine). Also states work is not 'directly and closely related' if remotely related or completely unrelated to exempt duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples of 'directly and closely related' work
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete examples illustrating when routine or seemingly nonexempt tasks are directly and closely related to exempt duties: (1) keeping time/production/sales records for subordinates; (2) distribution of materials/merchandise to control flow and expenditures; (3) supervisor spot checks/examinations distinguishable from nonexempt inspector work; (4) supervisor setting up machines may be exempt depending on industry/operation; (5) department manager observing sales floor performance; (6) consultant note-taking/typing necessary for analysis and recommendations; (7) credit manager administering credit policy and related record tasks; (8) traffic manager planning transportation and negotiating carriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numbered examples illustrate the application of 'directly and closely related' across industries and stress the context-dependent nature of whether a task is exemptly related (e.g., setup work may be exempt in some operations but part of production in others).
